title: A Brief History of Islamic Education in Singapore
subtitle: Rooted in Tradition. Shaped by Singapore.
introduction: Islamic education in Singapore has grown through generations of scholars, educators, philanthropists and institutions. Rooted in Islamic traditions and the local socio-religious context, it is enriched by scholarly networks across the Malay world and beyond.
This digital exhibition traces selected milestones from the 19th to the 21st century, highlighting a cosmopolitan and adaptive tradition.
Selected texts and manuscripts showcase Singapore’s Islamic intellectual heritage and SCIS’s commitment to its preservation and study through research and the Library’s Special Collections.
SCIS continues this intellectual legacy and opens a new chapter in Islamic education in Singapore.

milestones.title: A port connects people and ideas
milestones.description: Singapore's emergence as a major trading port in the 19th century attracted Muslim merchants, scholars and pilgrims from across the Malay world and beyond. These transregional networks facilitated not only the movement of people and goods, but also the circulation of religious knowledge, scholarly ideas and intellectual traditions, establishing Singapore as an important meeting point within the wider Muslim world.
milestones.imageAlt: Page of a manuscript supplied as the account by Kiyai Abdulrahman Klotok, with handwritten text and marginal notes.
milestones.caption: Hajj Travel Manuscript of Kiyai Abdulrahman Klotok (1837)
milestones.source: Kiyai Abdurrahman Klotok, a Javanese Islamic scholar from Bojonegoro, East Java, documented his pilgrimage journey to Mecca in a manuscript dating to 1837. Having travelled through Lingga and Riau, he arrived in Singapore on 22 October 1837, referring to the settlement as “Pulo Selat” under British administration. He remained in Singapore for approximately two months before departing for Jeddah on 5 December 1837. His account provides valuable early evidence of Singapore's role as a transit point for pilgrims and scholars from the Malay-Indonesian world, reflecting the maritime and religious networks connecting the region to the wider Muslim world. Image credit: Hajj travel manuscript of Kiyai Abdurrahman Klotok. Photograph courtesy of RPCS Research Fellow, Dr A. Ginanjar Sya’ban.

milestones.title: Learning takes root in the community
milestones.description: Mosques, homes and informal teaching circles became important centres of Islamic learning in early Singapore, sustained by ulama, Sufi networks and connections with the wider Muslim world. Singapore also attracted prominent scholars who produced religious writings on the island, including Sheikh Salim bin Sumayr and Sheikh Ismail al-Khalidi al-Minangkabawi, reflecting its emerging role as a centre of Islamic intellectual activity.
milestones.imageAlt: Page of Risalah ar-Radd ‘ala Ahl al-Tariqah, supplied as a work by Sheikh Salim bin Sumayr.
milestones.caption: Risalah ar-Radd ‘ala Ahl al-Tariqah — Sheikh Salim bin Sumayr. A religious treatise written in Singapore, reflecting the scholarly activity and religious discourses taking place on the island during the 19th century.
milestones.source: Written in Singapore in 1853 (1269 AH) by Sheikh Salim bin Sumair (d. 1857), this Arabic manuscript describes gatherings involving communal dhikr (remembrance of God) and extended periods of spiritual retreat (khalwah), reflecting debates over religious practices and interpretations of Islam. It provides valuable evidence of an active Islamic intellectual environment in mid-19th-century Singapore, where scholars engaged in theological discussions and contested religious ideas, highlighting the island's role as a centre of Islamic scholarship and intellectual exchange. Image source: Leiden University Libraries, MS Or. 6982.

displayObjects.source: Mawahib Rabb al-Falaq, an Arabic commentary on a religious poem by Nasir al-Din Ibn al-Milaq al-Shadhili, was written by Sheikh Isma‘il al-Khalidi al-Minangkabawi (d. 1858), a prominent Minangkabau scholar associated with the Shattari and Naqshbandi Sufi traditions. displayObjects.featureTitle: A Chinese Muslim Scholar in Singapore
displayObjects.featureText: The Chinese Muslim scholar from Yunnan, Yusuf Ma Dexin, recorded his stay in Singapore during the 1840s in his travelogue Chaojin Tuji (Record of the Pilgrimage Journey). His account illustrates Singapore's place within wider pilgrimage routes linking China, Southeast Asia and the Hijaz.

displayObjects.imageAlt: Opening spread of the Chinese woodblock edition of Chaojin Tuji, with vertical columns of text and a red seal.
displayObjects.caption: Chaojin Tuji (朝覲途記): Record of the Pilgrimage Journey (1861)
displayObjects.source: Chaojin Tuji documents the pilgrimage and scholarly travels of Sheikh Yusuf Ma Dexin (1794–1874), a prominent Chinese Muslim scholar from Yunnan, who journeyed through Southeast Asia, including Singapore, to Mecca and other centres of Islamic learning between 1841 and 1849. Originally written in Arabic, the account was translated into Chinese by his disciple Ma Anli and published in Kunming, China, in 1861. The text offers valuable insights into 19th-century pilgrimage routes, maritime connections and scholarly networks, highlighting Singapore's role as a transit point for Muslim pilgrims and scholars travelling between China, Southeast Asia and the wider Muslim world. Image: Extract from the 1861 Chinese woodblock-printed edition of Chaojin Tuji (朝覲途記), translated by Ma Anli. Collection of Tianjin Library, China.

milestones.title: A centre for the printed word
milestones.description: By the late 19th century, Singapore had emerged as a major centre of Islamic printing and publishing, particularly around Kampong Gelam, facilitating the production and circulation of Jawi religious texts across the Malay world. This flourishing print culture supported Islamic education by widening access to religious knowledge and strengthening intellectual networks. The works produced during this period reflect the diversity of 19th-century Singapore, where works in Arabic, Jawi, Pegon (Javanese written in Arabic-derived script), Tamil and other languages and scripts facilitated the transmission of religious knowledge across different communities. This multilingual print culture underscores Singapore's role as a cosmopolitan centre of Islamic learning, publishing and intellectual exchange.

The anthology contains 55 devotional poems praising Prophet Muhammad, spiritual leaders and Muslim saints (awliya).

milestones.title: Structured education expands
milestones.description: The early decades of the 20th century witnessed the emergence and expansion of formal madrasah education in Singapore, beginning with early institutions such as Madrasah As-Sibyan (1905) and Madrasah al-Iqbal (1908). This was followed by the establishment of six madrasahs that continue to operate today: Madrasah Alsagoff Al-Arabiah (1912), Madrasah Aljunied Al-Islamiah (1927), Madrasah Al-Arabiah Al-Islamiah (1930s), Madrasah Al-Ma'arif Al-Islamiah (1936), Madrasah Al-Irsyad Al-Islamiah (1947) and Madrasah Wak Tanjong Al-Islamiah (1955).

A pioneering female religious educator and advocate for women's education in Singapore, Ustazah Khamsiah became the first female principal (mudirah) of Madrasah Alsagoff Al-Arabiah in the early 1960s. Her leadership coincided with the madrasah's transformation into an all-girls institution in 1966, contributing to the expansion of formal Islamic education for girls. Beyond her administrative role, she was remembered for her dedication to teaching, mentorship and advancing educational opportunities for Muslim women.

milestones.title: Philanthropy and collective efforts sustain learning
milestones.description: Muslim benefactors and community organisations played an important role in sustaining and expanding Islamic education in Singapore through waqf, philanthropy, scholarships and community initiatives. Organisations such as Jamiyah, Muhammadiyah, PERGAS and Lembaga Biasiswa Kenangan Maulud (LBKM) contributed through religious education programmes, educational institutions, teacher development, scholarships and financial assistance. Alongside the support of individual philanthropists and community leaders, these efforts broadened access to Islamic education, strengthened religious learning and supported the educational advancement of the Muslim community.

displayObjects.modalTitle: Kiyai Fadhlullah Suhaimi (1886-1964). Kiyai Fadhlullah Suhaimi was a prominent ulama-intellectual, educator and reformist thinker who played a significant role in advancing Islamic education and intellectual discourse in Singapore. A strong advocate of women's education, he established Madrasah Al-Ma’arif in 1936, a pioneering institution that expanded opportunities for Muslim girls to pursue formal Islamic education. The Daughters of Kiyai Fadhlullah Suhaimi: Pioneers of Women's Islamic Education. The three daughters of Kiyai Fadhlullah Suhaimi—Saadah, Kamaliah and Saedah Suhaimi—were among the pioneering Muslim women from Singapore who pursued higher education in Egypt, reflecting their father's commitment to women's intellectual and educational advancement. Upon completing their studies, they contributed to Islamic education across Southeast Asia. Ustazah Saadah served as principal of Madrasah Al-Ma’arif for approximately two decades, continuing her father's educational legacy in Singapore. Ustazah Kamaliah taught at an Arabic school in Brunei, while Ustazah Saedah became an educator, lecturer and principal of Maahad Hamidiah in Selangor, where she also participated in religious administration. Their achievements demonstrate the expanding role of Muslim women as scholars, educators and institutional leaders, while highlighting the transregional networks connecting Singapore's Islamic educational heritage with Egypt and the wider Malay world.

highlights.label: A contemporary chapter in a continuing tradition

closing: From early centres of learning and regional scholarly networks to modern madrasahs and institutions of higher education, Singapore’s Islamic educational tradition continues to evolve.
This heritage reflects generations of intellectual exchange, community commitment and institutional development, providing foundations for the future of Islamic education in Singapore.
opening: From a bustling port connecting scholars, pilgrims and ideas across the Muslim world to the educational institutions of modern Singapore, Islamic education has evolved through generations of learning, intellectual exchange and renewal. Rooted in Islamic traditions, shaped by Singapore’s local context and enriched by global scholarly networks, this exhibition traces the people, institutions and milestones that have shaped its development and enduring intellectual heritage.
openingQuestion: What makes a place a meeting point for knowledge?

chapters.label: Connections
chapters.title: A Port of Trade. A Meeting Place of Knowledge.
chapters.question: What else travelled through 19th century Singapore besides goods and people?
chapters.historyDetail: As Singapore emerged as a bustling maritime trading port in the 19th century, it became not only a crossroads of commerce but also a meeting place for scholars, pilgrims, merchants and travellers from across the Malay world and beyond. As historian Michael Laffan observed in The Makings of Indonesian Islam, “There (Singapore) the pilgrim, the jurist, and the Sufi could all meet.” Alongside the movement of goods and people came the circulation of religious texts, scholarly traditions and intellectual ideas, connecting Singapore to established centres of Islamic learning across the wider Muslim world. Mosques, homes and informal teaching circles served as important spaces for religious learning.

chapters.label: Transformation
chapters.title: A Changing Society. An Evolving Education.
chapters.intro: At the turn of the 20th century, Singapore had emerged as a vibrant centre of Islamic printing, publishing and intellectual discourse, embedded within transregional scholarly networks connecting Java, Riau and Sumatra with major centres of Islamic learning such as Mecca, Cairo and Istanbul. The circulation of religious treatises, newspapers and periodicals facilitated the exchange of ideas and stimulated discussions on religious reform, the modernisation of Islamic education and the expansion of educational opportunities for women and girls.
chapters.question: How significant was Singapore's role as a centre of printing and intellectual exchange in the Malay world?
chapters.historyDetail: Singapore emerged as a major centre of Malay-language printing and publishing, facilitating the production and circulation of religious texts, literature and intellectual ideas across the Malay world. Between 1921 and 1949, Singapore accounted for 119 of the 243 publishing and printing establishments (approximately 49%) recorded across Malaya and Singapore, reflecting its prominence within the regional publishing landscape.
chapters.featureText: One of Singapore's earliest documented madrasahs, Madrasah As-Sibyan (1905), had connections to the Muslim printing community of Kampong Gelam. Muhammad bin Muhammad Sa'id, who was associated with the madrasah as a teacher, was the son of Haji Muhammad Sa'id bin Haji Arsyad, a prominent printer and publisher of Malay and Islamic texts. This connection illustrates how Singapore's flourishing Islamic print culture and early madrasah education were intertwined in the transmission of religious knowledge.

chapters.label: Continuity & Renewal
chapters.title: A Living Tradition. A Shared Future.
chapters.intro: Lifelong learning and higher education extend the story beyond the classroom. The professional development of religious educators and the establishment of SCIS are contemporary chapters in a tradition that continues to evolve.
chapters.question: What does it mean to prepare religious scholars for the Singapore of tomorrow?

7.title: Institutions in a changing Singapore
7.text: The exhibition’s post-independence account follows educational coordination through MUIS (1968), MENDAKI (1982) and the Islamic Education Advisory Board (1990). These dates locate institutional development within Singapore’s changing national story.
7.basis: Dates from milestone 7. Chronological context does not establish a particular policy or causal relationship.

12.title: Scholarship in a plural society
12.text: The SCIS milestone places Islamic scholarship alongside interdisciplinary research and Singapore’s socio-religious context. It invites us to consider how an inherited intellectual tradition engages with the society in which it lives.
12.basis: Interpretation of milestone 12; SCIS is one contemporary chapter, not an inevitable endpoint.

archiveNotes.3: Javanese Muslim printers and publishers played a pioneering role in establishing Singapore as a major centre of Islamic printing and intellectual exchange during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Figures such as Haji Muhammad Said (H.M. Said), Haji Muhammad Siraj (H.M. Siraj) and Haji Muhammad Amin (H.M. Amin) were among those associated with the growth of Muslim printing and publishing enterprises, particularly around Kampong Gelam. These early Muslim printers and publishers laid important foundations for Singapore’s Islamic intellectual heritage, helping transform the port city into a regional centre for the production, circulation and exchange of religious knowledge.
archiveNotes.8: This thematic milestone begins in the 1960s and also mentions the Joint Madrasah System in 2009. “Onwards” describes a continuing theme, not a single event.

closingReflection: Singapore’s Islamic educational heritage is a story of continuity and change. Across generations, its scholars, educators and institutions have preserved knowledge, responded to new circumstances and contributed to the life of the community.
As Singapore continues to evolve, this living tradition reminds us that heritage is not only what we inherit, but also what we carry forward.

objects.imageAlt: Historical group photograph with a Jawi caption. Haji Abbas Taha is seated second from left.
objects.caption: Haji Abbas bin Muhammad Taha (1885-1954) (seated, second from left) was a prominent Singapore-born ulama-intellectual, educator and journalist who contributed significantly to Islamic scholarship and intellectual discourse in the early 20th century. He served as a religious teacher, Kadi of Tanjong Pagar and later Chief Kadi of Singapore (1936). He was assistant editor and subsequently editor of Al-Imam (1906–1908), before founding and editing Neracha (1911–1915) and Tunas Melayu (1913).
